slides.title: Principle and purpose
bullets: Glucose is one of the main components of blood; its level reflects carbohydrate metabolism in the body.
Glucose oxidase (GOD) turns glucose into gluconic acid and hydrogen peroxide.
In the presence of peroxidase (POD) hydrogen peroxide reacts with phenol and 4-aminoantipyrine to form red quinoneimine.
The intensity of the colour (measured at 505 nm) is proportional to the amount of glucose.

slides.title: Specimen and reagents
bullets: Specimen: serum; EDTA or heparin plasma.
R1 — buffer (phosphate buffer, phenol); R2 — substrate (glucose oxidase, peroxidase, 4-aminoantipyrine); R3 — standard: glucose 5.56 mmol/L (100 mg/dL).
Working reagent: dissolve the R2 substrate in the R1 buffer carefully.
Stability: 6 months at 2–8 °C, 3 weeks at 15–25 °C; keep protected from light.
The volumes, times and concentrations given belong to the kit named in the manual (Hospitex Diagnostics); with another kit follow its instructions.

slides.title: Procedure (manual)
rows: 505 nm, 37 °C, 1 cm cuvette, zero against reagent

slides.title: Calculation and result
bullets: The colour is stable for 60 minutes. Volumes in brackets are for a standard cuvette.
Glucose (mmol/L) = sample absorbance / standard absorbance × standard concentration.
Linearity: up to 27.8 mmol/L (500 mg/dL); samples with a higher concentration are diluted with distilled water and the result multiplied by the dilution.

slides.title: Calculation and result
bullets: Reference range in the manual: 3.61–6.11 mmol/L (65–110 mg/dL); Saidov and Isajanov also write that blood glucose stays at about 3.6–6.1 mmol/L. Each laboratory applies its own reference range.

Raised glucose (hyperglycaemia): diabetes mellitus, endocrine disease, pancreatic disease, chronic liver and kidney disease and others; lowered (hypoglycaemia): excess insulin, some endocrine disorders, severe poisoning.

slides.title: Sources of error and quality control
bullets: The colour is light-sensitive: keep the working reagent protected from light and do not use it past its date.
Standard and sample must be treated under the same conditions (temperature, incubation time); volumes are measured with sound pipettes.
A haemolysed, turbid or lipaemic sample may distort the result — take a new one.
If the result is above the limit of linearity, dilute the sample and repeat.
Quality control: measure the control material in every analytical series and record the result on the control chart.

slides.title: Reagent preparation (for a semi-automatic analyser)
bullets: Working reagent: dissolve the R2 substrate in the R1 buffer carefully; stable for 6 months at 2–8 °C and 3 weeks at 15–25 °C, keep away from light.
Calibration: by standard — the R3 standard, glucose 5.56 mmol/L (100 mg/dL).
Mode — end point: read after 15 minutes of incubation at 37 °C; the colour is stable for 60 minutes.

slides.title: Reagent preparation (for a semi-automatic analyser)
bullets: Zero: against water in the programme table, against reagent in the manual conditions — set up the reagent blank as the kit IFU says.

The values belong to the Hospitex Diagnostics kit and the Screen Master Plus photometer in the manual. The IFU of the kit you use and the analyser manual always take precedence — check the parameters against them.

slides.title: Semi-automatic analyser: glucose programme
rows: Rows are shifted in the electronic copy — not readable; manual: 15 minutes at 37 °C

slides.title: Safety
bullets: Serum and plasma are potentially infectious: wear single-use or rubber gloves.
Never pipette material by mouth.
Disinfect used cuvettes, tubes and tips (according to the regulation in force).
Reagents are for in vitro diagnostic use only.

slides.eyebrow: Carbohydrate metabolism · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Plasma  ·  Units: mg/dL, mmol/L  ·  Population: Not pregnant
What it is used for: Screening for prediabetes and diabetes, finding the cause of symptoms of high or low glucose, and monitoring side effects of some long-term medicines that affect glucose.

slides.title: Fasting plasma glucose
slides.eyebrow: Carbohydrate metabolism · Reference values and decision limits · 1/2
rows: People who are not pregnant, after fasting for at least 8 hours
People who are not pregnant (WHO/IDF criteria) — WHO: 6.1–6.9 mmol/L; 2-hour glucose, if measured, < 7.8 mmol/L. The ADA/NIDDK lower limit is 100 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L).

slides.title: Fasting plasma glucose
slides.eyebrow: Carbohydrate metabolism · Reference values and decision limits · 2/2
rows: People who are not pregnant, after fasting for at least 8 hours — Diagnosis usually requires a repeat test. Pregnancy uses different criteria.

slides.title: Fasting plasma glucose
cols: Prediabetes and diabetes are the most common causes. Other possible causes include an overactive thyroid gland (hyperthyroidism), pancreatic problems including pancreatitis, stress from surgery, very serious illness or trauma, adrenal gland problems and certain medicines.
With diabetes: some diabetes medicines and other glucose-lowering medicines, not eating enough (especially after taking diabetes medicine) and more physical activity than usual.

slides.title: Fasting plasma glucose
cols: Without diabetes, low glucose is uncommon; possible causes include liver or kidney disease, underactive adrenal glands, some pituitary disorders, an underactive thyroid gland (hypothyroidism), malnutrition, certain medicines and alcohol use disorder.

slides.title: Fasting plasma glucose
bullets: Limitations: What a result means depends on which test was done, other test results and the medical history.
